title: Skills transition: Lawyer growth coexists with clerical decline
desc: Combines differentiated occupational forecasts with employer plans for automation, augmentation and training, not universal displacement.

kps.k: The cluster frames technological change as workforce restructuring and adaptation, not a direct forecast of AI-driven job elimination.
kps.d: The Future of Jobs Report 2025 draws on employers’ 2024 expectations through 2030. Respondents expect predominantly human task shares to fall from 48% to 33%, predominantly technological shares to rise from 22% to 34%, and combined work to rise from 30% to 33%. These task allocations do not translate into equivalent job losses. The report places AI alongside economic, demographic and other technological drivers; its 22% structural labour-force churn combines job creation and loss rather than measuring net displacement. The supplied material contains varied employer expectations, not a direct exchange between opposing positions or a causal estimate of AI’s employment effects.

kps.k: Employers plan to pursue automation, augmentation and workforce development together.
kps.d: Global comparators show 85% planning upskilling, 73% accelerated automation, 70% hiring for emerging skills, 63% technological augmentation and 51% transitions from declining to growing roles. In response specifically to AI, 77% plan to train existing workers to work alongside it and 47% plan internal transitions from jobs they expect AI to shrink. These intentions make adaptation central to the report’s account, but do not establish successful implementation or guarantee that redeployment will offset displacement.

kps.k: Skills shortages constrain transformation, while substantial training needs leave some workers at risk of missing the transition.
kps.d: The report identifies labour-market skills gaps as the leading perceived barrier, cited by 63% of employers globally. Its representative group of 100 workers includes 29 expected to upskill within their roles, 19 to upskill and redeploy, and 11 unlikely to upskill; 41 would need no training. Employers anticipate productivity, competitiveness and retention benefits, but the survey does not demonstrate those returns. Constraints also differ by sector: healthcare employers rank organisational culture and resistance first, whereas real-estate employers prioritise difficulty attracting industry talent. The practical implication is that training alone may not address employers’ reported obstacles.

kps.k: The occupational forecasts distinguish modest lawyer growth from clerical decline and rapid expansion in AI-related roles.
kps.d: The report projects global net growth of 2% for lawyers over 2025–2030, against 82% for AI and machine-learning specialists and declines of 20% for administrative assistants and executive secretaries and 18% for accounting, bookkeeping and payroll clerks. Lawyer forecasts vary geographically: Canada anticipates 3% growth, South-eastern Asia 6%, and Kazakhstan a 5% decline. These forecasts provide context for the legal-AI labour debate, but neither establish observed displacement nor predict changes in law-firm leverage, junior recruitment or staffing structures.

kps.k: Employers favour training support and broader talent measures, without implying a universal policy package or automatic labour-cost savings.
kps.d: Employers globally identify training funding (55%), training provision (52%) and improved public education (47%) as promising ways to increase talent availability. Priorities vary: Slovenia favours hiring and firing flexibility, while Zimbabwe favours education. Business priorities also encompass well-being, progression and diverse talent pools. Meanwhile, 52% expect compensation to grow as a share of revenue and 41% expect a similar share, which cautions against reading automation plans as uniform cost-reduction forecasts. These figures measure preferences and expectations—not intervention effectiveness or individual wage growth. Missing headings and interleaved extraction limit precise interpretation of some profile figures.

vlens.an: Within this curated professional voice, the Future of Jobs Report 2025 supports the proposition that technological change is expected to produce differentiated workforce restructuring rather than universal AI-driven job elimination. Its employer-survey forecasts distinguish modest global lawyer growth from much faster growth in AI-related roles and declines in clerical occupations. It also shows employers planning automation alongside augmentation, upskilling, hiring and redeployment, making adaptation—not simple substitution—the central response. Material variation remains: lawyer forecasts differ by geography, some workers are expected to miss the skills transition, and sector-specific barriers extend beyond skills gaps to culture and talent attraction. These are employers’ expectations for 2025–2030, not observed outcomes or causal evidence that AI alone produces the forecast changes.

elens.an: The 2025 source supports the proposition that technological adoption is expected to produce differentiated workforce restructuring rather than universal AI-driven job elimination. Its employer-survey forecasts distinguish modest global growth for lawyers from much faster growth in AI-related roles and decline in clerical occupations. It also presents automation, technological augmentation, hiring and upskilling as concurrent strategies, making adaptation—not simple substitution—the central mechanism. Material variation qualifies but does not reverse that support: lawyer forecasts differ geographically, sectoral barriers range from skills shortages to organisational resistance and talent attraction, and some workers are expected to miss the training transition. The evidence remains prospective: it reports employers’ 2024 expectations and plans through 2030, not observed adoption outcomes, causal effects attributable to AI alone, or demonstrated success in retraining and redeployment. Because the corpus contains one curated source for this period, its position should not be generalized to employers as a whole.
